sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, forced treatment, restraint and deaths in psychiatric hospitals. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Psychiatric hospitals and the psychiatric units of general hospitals are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track them as facilities. This page is about acute inpatient care for adults and young people: hospital stays, often after a crisis and often involuntary. Youth psychiatric residential treatment facilities (PRTFs) and residential treatment centers are part of the troubled teen industry. They are in [our directory](/tti-program-index/), not on this page.

We made this page because the two meet. The largest for-profit chains run both psychiatric hospitals and youth residential programs, and the same practices and the same pressure to fill beds are documented in both. We are not the experts on psychiatric hospitals. The organizations listed below are, and many of them are run by people who have been hospitalized themselves.

sections.label: What the industry is
sections.heading: What psychiatric hospitals are
sections.body:
Inpatient psychiatric care happens in three kinds of place: free-standing psychiatric hospitals, psychiatric units inside general hospitals (often called psych wards), and state and county hospitals. When Medicare began in 1965, state and local hospitals provided most of this care. In 2023, [only 4 percent of Medicare-covered psychiatric hospital days were in government-run free-standing hospitals, and 35 percent were in privately owned ones](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Mar25_Ch13_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf#page=3). The rest were in general hospital units.

Medicare counted [1,430 certified inpatient psychiatric facilities in fiscal year 2024](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/July2026_MedPAC_DataBook_Sec6_SEC.pdf#page=22), down from 1,610 in 2019. Of these, 59 percent were units inside general hospitals. Over a quarter were free-standing for-profit hospitals, up from about one-fifth in 2019. A 2024 national survey of treatment facilities counted [60,201 inpatient mental health beds](https://www.kff.org/mental-health/state-indicator/count-and-rate-per-100000-of-mental-health-treatment-facility-beds-by-type/) for all ages.

Medicaid, Medicare, private insurance and state budgets pay for this care. Acadia Healthcare, one of the two largest for-profit chains, received [57.7 percent of its 2025 revenue from Medicaid and 14.3 percent from Medicare](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1520697/000119312526078266/achc-20251231.htm).

Many admissions are involuntary. States allow emergency holds for evaluation and court-ordered commitment, under rules and time limits that differ from state to state, and there is no national count. A study published in *Psychiatric Services* in 2020 used data from 24 states with 52 percent of the population and found [357 emergency involuntary detentions per 100,000 people in 2014](https://www.uclahealth.org/news/release/study-finds-involuntary-psychiatric-detentions-on-the-rise), about 591,000 detentions in those states alone. In 22 states with data for 2012 to 2016, the detention rate rose 13 percent while the population grew 4 percent.

sections.label: Where it meets the TTI
sections.heading: Where it meets the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### The same companies

Universal Health Services (UHS) runs one of the largest networks of psychiatric hospitals in the country. Its annual report for 2025 lists [182 inpatient behavioral health facilities in the United States](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/352915/000119312526071676/uhs-20251231.htm), plus 161 in the United Kingdom and 3 in Puerto Rico. The same list includes psychiatric hospitals and youth programs such as Provo Canyon School and Copper Hills Youth Center in Utah and Oak Plains Academy in Tennessee. In some places a hospital and a residential treatment center share a name: Cedar Ridge Behavioral Hospital and Cedar Ridge Residential Treatment Center in Oklahoma City, and North Star Hospital in Anchorage with the North Star DeBarr and Palmer residential treatment centers. Our records list 75 programs under [Universal Health Services](/operator/universal-health-services/).

Acadia Healthcare ran [277 behavioral health facilities with over 12,500 beds in 40 states and Puerto Rico](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1520697/000119312526078266/achc-20251231.htm) at the end of 2025. Not counting its addiction clinics, about 60 percent are acute psychiatric hospitals and 9 percent are residential treatment centers. The company writes that the children and adolescents in those centers "typically have had multiple prior failed treatment plans," and that stays run from three months to several years. Our records list 14 programs under [Acadia Healthcare](/operator/acadia-healthcare/).

### The same practices

Federal rules for hospitals forbid restraint or seclusion ["imposed as a means of coercion, discipline, convenience, or retaliation by staff"](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/482.13). They count a drug given to manage a patient's behavior, when it is not a standard treatment or dose for the patient's condition, as a restraint, and they require hospitals to report to CMS every death that happens in restraint or seclusion or within 24 hours after it. Physical restraint, seclusion and drugs used to control behavior are the same practices documented in troubled teen programs.

In 2024 the U.S. Senate Finance Committee published *Warehouses of Neglect*, a two-year investigation of youth residential treatment run by UHS, Acadia, Devereux and Vivant. It found that these providers ["optimize per diems by filling large facilities to capacity and maximize profit by concurrently reducing the number and quality of staff"](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/sfc_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf#page=4). Asked whether a child could be chemically restrained and secluded at once, UHS personnel told committee staff ["there are no rules preventing doubling or tripling up on a restraint and seclusion."](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/sfc_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf#page=58) The report notes that the practice is prohibited by federal regulations. Investigators and reporters have described the same pressure to fill beds in the companies' psychiatric hospitals (see below).

### Providers outside the industry

We keep a separate [list of mental health providers](/mental-health-providers/) outside the troubled teen industry, such as psychiatric units, that use its practices or refer young people to its programs.

sections.label: What investigations found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **1998 to 1999, restraint deaths.** The Hartford Courant's 1998 series "Deadly Restraint" counted 142 deaths tied to restraint or seclusion over ten years in psychiatric hospitals, psychiatric wards, group homes and youth residential facilities. A [1999 GAO report](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GAOREPORTS-HEHS-99-176/pdf/GAOREPORTS-HEHS-99-176.pdf) requested by members of Congress found that only 15 states had any system to alert their Protection and Advocacy agency to such deaths, identified 24 deaths in fiscal year 1998 from partial records, and said many more may occur. It found that until 1999 no federal rules governed restraint and seclusion in psychiatric hospitals.
- **2006, unreported deaths.** The HHS Inspector General found that [hospitals failed to report to CMS 44 of 104 documented deaths](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2006/hospital-reporting-of-deaths-related-to-restraint-and-seclusion/) related to restraint and seclusion between August 1999 and December 2004, and that CMS and state survey agencies often did not act on reported deaths in time.
- **2016, UHS.** A BuzzFeed News investigation, based on interviews with 175 current and former UHS staff, reported that [employees at UHS psychiatric hospitals described pressure to fill beds and to keep patients until their insurance ran out](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/rosalindadams/intake). UHS rejected the allegations.
- **2020, UHS settlement.** UHS and related entities agreed to [pay $122 million](https://www.oversight.gov/universal-health-services-inc-and-related-entities-pay-122-million-settle-false-claims-act-0) to settle False Claims Act allegations that from 2006 to 2018 its behavioral health facilities admitted patients who did not need inpatient care, kept them longer than needed, understaffed, and improperly used physical and chemical restraints and seclusion. Liability was not determined. UHS signed a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with an independent monitor for its behavioral health division.
- **2024, Acadia.** A New York Times investigation reported that [Acadia held patients against their will when it was not medically necessary](https://www.sltrib.com/news/2024/09/02/acadia-healthcare-holds/), often for financial reasons rather than medical ones, according to more than 50 current and former executives and staff. In at least 12 of the 19 states where Acadia runs psychiatric hospitals, patients, employees and police officers had alerted authorities. In September 2024 Acadia paid $19.9 million, admitting no liability, to settle a federal investigation of [medical necessity, admissions, discharges, length of stay and patient care](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1520697/000119312526078266/achc-20251231.htm) at several of its facilities.
- **2024 to 2026, federal investigations of Acadia.** Since September 2024 Acadia has received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department's Criminal Division about the admissions, length of stay and billing of its acute psychiatric hospitals, and subpoenas from the SEC. As of [its July 2026 quarterly report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1520697/000119312526321076/achc-20260630.htm), the investigations were open, no findings had been made, and the company said it was cooperating.

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text [988](tel:988), the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 24 hours a day.
- **Protection and Advocacy agency.** Every state and territory has one. Under the federal PAIMI program they [investigate abuse, neglect and rights violations](https://www.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/paimi-activities-report-fy-19-20.pdf) against people with mental illness in public and private facilities, including restraint and seclusion. Find yours in [NDRN's directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **State health department.** Hospitals are licensed by the state, and the state survey agency investigates complaints for Medicare and Medicaid. CMS lists [each state's complaint contact](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information).
- **The Joint Commission**, if the hospital is accredited by it: [report a safety concern online](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/contact-us/report-a-patient-safety-event) or call 1-800-994-6610. You can report anonymously.
- **A death in restraint or seclusion** must be reported by the hospital to CMS. You can also tell the state survey agency and the Protection and Advocacy agency yourself.
- For troubled teen programs, including youth residential treatment run by the same companies, use [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [MindFreedom International](https://mindfreedom.org/): A human rights organization in mental health care, with psychiatric survivors among its board and past leaders. It works against forced psychiatric treatment.
- [National Association for Rights Protection and Advocacy (NARPA)](https://www.narpa.org/): Supports people with psychiatric diagnoses in exercising their legal and human rights, and works to end forced treatment.
- [National Empowerment Center](https://power2u.org/): Works with people with lived experience of mental health issues, trauma and extreme states. It keeps directories of peer respites and peer-run warmlines.
- [Wildflower Alliance](https://wildfloweralliance.org/): A grassroots group in Western Massachusetts and online offering peer support, advocacy and training, including peer-run respites.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/): The national organization of the Protection and Advocacy agencies, the largest providers of legal advocacy for people with disabilities.
- [Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law](https://www.bazelon.org/): A national legal advocacy organization for the civil rights of people with mental disabilities, through lawsuits and policy work.
- [Mad in America](https://www.madinamerica.com/): A publication of the Mad in America Foundation with research news, original journalism and writing by people with lived experience of psychiatric care.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you have been hospitalized, work in psychiatric care or advocate in this field, and something on this page is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will change it.
